questions.question_text: The ratio of momentum of the photons of the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ line of Balmer series of Hydrogen atoms is $\alpha/\beta$ . The possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are:-
questions.question_html: The ratio of momentum of the photons of the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ line of Balmer series of Hydrogen atoms is $\alpha/\beta$ . The possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are:-
questions.explanation_text: According to the de Broglie relation, the momentum (p) of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength ( $\lambda$ ): $p=\frac{h}{\lambda}$ Therefore, the ratio of momenta is the inverse ratio of their wavelengths: $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}$ The Balmer series occurs when an electron transitions from a higher energy level $(n_{2})$ to the second energy level ( $n_{1}=2$ ). The wavelength is given by Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{n^{2}})$ For $1^{\text{st}}$ line of Balmer transition from $n=3$ to $n=2$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9})=R(\frac{9-4}{36})=\frac{5R}{36} \Rightarrow \lambda_{1}=\frac{36}{5R}$ For $2^{nd}$ line of Balmer transition from $n=4$ to $n=2$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}}=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16})=R(\frac{4-1}{16})=\frac{3R}{16} \Rightarrow \lambda_{2}=\frac{16}{3R}$ So, the ratio $(\alpha/\beta)$ , $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{16/3R}{36/5R}=\frac{16}{3} \times \frac{5}{36}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{4 \times 5}{3 \times 9}=\frac{20}{27}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ So, $\alpha=20$ and $\beta=27$ . Therefore, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
According to the de Broglie relation, the momentum (p) of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength ( $\lambda$ ):

$p=\frac{h}{\lambda}$

Therefore, the ratio of momenta is the inverse ratio of their wavelengths:

$\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}$

The Balmer series occurs when an electron transitions from a higher energy level $(n_{2})$ to the second energy level ( $n_{1}=2$ ). The wavelength is given by Rydberg formula:

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{n^{2}})$

For $1^{\text{st}}$ line of Balmer transition from $n=3$ to $n=2$ .

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9})=R(\frac{9-4}{36})=\frac{5R}{36} \Rightarrow \lambda_{1}=\frac{36}{5R}$

For $2^{nd}$ line of Balmer transition from $n=4$ to $n=2$ .

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}}=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16})=R(\frac{4-1}{16})=\frac{3R}{16} \Rightarrow \lambda_{2}=\frac{16}{3R}$

So, the ratio $(\alpha/\beta)$ ,

$\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{16/3R}{36/5R}=\frac{16}{3} \times \frac{5}{36}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{4 \times 5}{3 \times 9}=\frac{20}{27}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$

So, $\alpha=20$ and $\beta=27$ .

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?
questions.question_html: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?
questions.explanation_text: Atoms are represented by the notation $X_{Z}^{A}$ , where : 1. A is the Mass Number (total number of protons and neutrons). 2. $Z$ is the Atomic Number (number of protons). Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z). Option A : $H_{1}^{3}$ and $He_{2}^{3}$ Mass numbers: 3 and 3 (Same) Atomic numbers: 1 and 2 (Different) Since they have the same mass number ( $A=3$ ) but represent different elements ( $Z=1$ vs $Z=2$ ), they are Isobars. Hence, option (A) is correct. Option B : $Hg_{80}^{198}$ and $Au_{79}^{197}$ Mass numbers: 198 and 197 (Different) Atomic numbers: 80 and 79 (Different) So, $Hg_{80}^{198}$ and $Au_{79}^{197}$ are neither isobars nor isotopes. Hence, option (B) is incorrect. Option C : $H_{1}^{2}$ and $H_{1}^{3}$ Mass numbers: 2 and 3 (Different) Atomic numbers: 1 and 1 (Same) So, $H_{1}^{2}$ and $H_{1}^{3}$ are Isotopes of Hydrogen (Deuterium and Tritium). Hence, option (C) is incorrect. Option D : $U_{92}^{236}$ and $U_{92}^{238}$ Mass numbers: 236 and 238 (Different) Atomic numbers: 92 and 92 (Same) So, $U_{92}^{236}$ and $U_{92}^{238}$ are Isotopes (same element, different mass) not isobars. Hence, option (D) is incorrect.

questions.question_text: The average energy released per fission for the nucleus of $_{92}^{235}U$ is 190 MeV . When all the atoms of 47 g pure $_{92}^{235}U$ undergo fission process, the energy released is $\alpha \times 10^{23}MeV$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . (Avogadro Number $=6 \times 10^{23}$ per mole)
questions.question_html:
The average energy released per fission for the nucleus of $_{92}^{235}U$ is 190 MeV . When all the atoms of 47 g pure $_{92}^{235}U$ undergo fission process, the energy released is $\alpha \times 10^{23}MeV$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

(Avogadro Number $=6 \times 10^{23}$ per mole)
questions.explanation_text: The number of moles (n) is given by the formula : $n=\frac{\text{Given Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}}$ Given : Mass of Uranium $=47g$ Molar Mass of $U_{92}^{235}=235g/mol$ $n=\frac{47}{235}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2moles$ Each mole contains a number of atoms equal to Avogadro's Number ( $N_{A}$ ). $N=n \times N_{A}$ $\Rightarrow$ $N=0.2 \times (6 \times 10^{23})$ Since each atom (nucleus) releases 190 MeV upon fission : $E=N \times \text{Energy per fission}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.2 \times 10^{23}) \times 190MeV$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=228 \times 10^{23}MeV$ $\Rightarrow \alpha \times 10^{23}MeV=228 \times 10^{23}MeV$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=228$ Therefore, the correct answer is $𝟐𝟐𝟖$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The number of moles (n) is given by the formula :

$n=\frac{\text{Given Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}}$

Given :

  • Mass of Uranium $=47g$

  • Molar Mass of $U_{92}^{235}=235g/mol$

$n=\frac{47}{235}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2moles$

Each mole contains a number of atoms equal to Avogadro's Number ( $N_{A}$ ).

$N=n \times N_{A}$

$\Rightarrow$ $N=0.2 \times (6 \times 10^{23})$

Since each atom (nucleus) releases 190 MeV upon fission :

$E=N \times \text{Energy per fission}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.2 \times 10^{23}) \times 190MeV$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=228 \times 10^{23}MeV$

$\Rightarrow \alpha \times 10^{23}MeV=228 \times 10^{23}MeV$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=228$

Therefore, the correct answer is $𝟐𝟐𝟖$ .

questions.question_text: Assuming the experimental mass of $_{6}^{12}C$ as $12u$ , the mass defect of $_{6}^{12}C$ atom is $____$ $MeV/c^{2}$ . (Mass of proton $=1.00727u$ . mass of neutron $=1.00866u,1u=931.5MeV/c^{2}$ and c is the speed of the light in vacuum).
questions.question_html:
Assuming the experimental mass of $_{6}^{12}C$ as $12u$ , the mass defect of $_{6}^{12}C$ atom is $____$ $MeV/c^{2}$ .

(Mass of proton $=1.00727u$ . mass of neutron $=1.00866u,1u=931.5MeV/c^{2}$ and c is the speed of the light in vacuum).
questions.explanation_text: Mass defect $(\Delta m)$ is the difference between the sum of the masses of the individual nucleons (protons and neutrons) and the actual experimental mass of the nucleus. For the atom $C_{6}^{12}$ , atomic number is $Z=6$ (Number of protons) Mass number is $A=12$ Number of neutrons $N=A-Z=12-6=6$ So, mass of 6 protons $=6 \times 1.00727u=6.04362u$ And the mass of 6 neutrons $=6 \times 1.00866u=6.05196u$ So, total theoretical mass $=6.04362+6.05196=12.09558u$ It is given that the experimental mass of $C_{6}^{12}=12u$ : Hence, the mass defect is $\Delta m=\text{(Total theoretical mass)}-\text{(Experimental mass)}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=12.09558u-12u=0.09558u$ The energy equivalent of 1 u is given as $931.5MeV/c^{2}$ . $\Delta m(\text{in}MeV/c^{2})=0.09558 \times 931.5$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m \approx 89.03277 \approx 89.03MeV/c^{\wedge}2$ Therefore, the mass defect of the $C_{6}^{12}$ atom is approximately $89.03MeV/c^{2}$ . Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
Mass defect $(\Delta m)$ is the difference between the sum of the masses of the individual nucleons (protons and neutrons) and the actual experimental mass of the nucleus.

For the atom $C_{6}^{12}$ , atomic number is $Z=6$ (Number of protons)

Mass number is $A=12$

Number of neutrons $N=A-Z=12-6=6$

So, mass of 6 protons $=6 \times 1.00727u=6.04362u$

And the mass of 6 neutrons $=6 \times 1.00866u=6.05196u$

So, total theoretical mass $=6.04362+6.05196=12.09558u$

It is given that the experimental mass of $C_{6}^{12}=12u$ :

Hence, the mass defect is

$\Delta m=\text{(Total theoretical mass)}-\text{(Experimental mass)}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=12.09558u-12u=0.09558u$

The energy equivalent of 1 u is given as $931.5MeV/c^{2}$ .

$\Delta m(\text{in}MeV/c^{2})=0.09558 \times 931.5$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m \approx 89.03277 \approx 89.03MeV/c^{\wedge}2$

Therefore, the mass defect of the $C_{6}^{12}$ atom is approximately $89.03MeV/c^{2}$ .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: In hydrogen atom spectrum, ( $R \rightarrow$ Rydberg's constant) A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3R}$ B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$ D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4R}$ Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.question_html:
In hydrogen atom spectrum, ( $R \rightarrow$ Rydberg's constant)

A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3R}$

B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum

C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$

D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4R}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.html: B, D Only

options.label: C
options.html: A, B and D Only

questions.explanation_text: Using the Rydberg formula : $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$ Where, $\lambda$ is the wavelength of radiated photon when electron makes a transition from initial energy state $n_{2}$ to final energy state $n_{1}$ , and R is the Rydberg's constant. For statement A The given series is Lyman ( $n_{1}=1$ ). Maximum wavelength implies minimum energy. The transition corresponds to the smallest energy gap, which is between the first excited state ( $n_{2}=2$ ) and the ground state ( $n_{1}=1$ ). $\frac{1}{\lambda_{max}}=R(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{2^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{max}}=R(1-\frac{1}{4})=\frac{3R}{4} \Rightarrow \lambda_{max}=\frac{4}{3R}$ Hence, the statement A is true. For statement B The given series is Balmer ( $n_{1}=2$ ). The Balmer series corresponds to electron transitions from higher shells ( $n=3,4,5\dots$ ) to the second shell $(n=2)$ . The wavelengths produced (e.g., $656nm,486nm)$ fall within the range of approximately 400 nm to 700 nm , which is the visible spectrum So, Balmer series lines are indeed visible. Hence, the statement B is true. For Statement C The given series is Paschen ( $n_{1}=3$ ). Minimum wavelength implies maximum energy. The transition corresponds to the largest energy gap, which is from infinity $(n_{2}=\infty)$ to the level $n_{1}=3$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda_{min}}=R(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{min}}=R(\frac{1}{9})=\frac{R}{9} \Rightarrow \lambda_{min}=\frac{9}{R}$ Hence, the statement C is also true. For statement D The given series is Lyman ( $n_{1}=1$ ). Minimum wavelength means ( $n_{2}=\infty \rightarrow n_{1}=1$ ). $\frac{1}{\lambda_{min}}=R(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{min}}=R(1-0)=R$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda_{min}=1R$ Hence, the statement D is false. Statement A is Correct. Statement B is Correct. Statement C is Correct. Statement D is Incorrect. Therefore, the correct option is (D).

For statement A

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{max}}=R(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{2^{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{max}}=R(1-\frac{1}{4})=\frac{3R}{4} \Rightarrow \lambda_{max}=\frac{4}{3R}$

Hence, the statement A is true.

For statement B

The given series is Balmer ( $n_{1}=2$ ).

The Balmer series corresponds to electron transitions from higher shells ( $n=3,4,5\dots$ ) to the second shell $(n=2)$ . The wavelengths produced (e.g., $656nm,486nm)$ fall within the range of approximately 400 nm to 700 nm , which is the visible spectrum

So, Balmer series lines are indeed visible. Hence, the statement B is true.

For Statement C

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers 200 and 212 respectively, shows spontaneous $\alpha$ -decay with same $Q$ value of 1 MeV . The ratio of energies of $\alpha$ -rays produced by A and B is $____$ .
questions.question_html: Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers 200 and 212 respectively, shows spontaneous $\alpha$ -decay with same $Q$ value of 1 MeV . The ratio of energies of $\alpha$ -rays produced by A and B is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: In $\alpha$ -decay, a parent nucleus (X) of mass number A decays into a daughter nucleus (Y) and an $\alpha$ -particle (Helium nucleus, mass number 4). $X_{Z}^{A} \rightarrow Y_{Z-2}^{A-4}+He_{2}^{4}$ Using conservation of momentum, the momentum of the $\alpha$ -particle ( $p_{\alpha}$ ) must be equal and opposite to the momentum of the daughter nucleus $(p_{D})$ . And using energy balance ( Q -value) the total kinetic energy released ( Q ) is shared between the $\alpha$ -particle and the daughter nucleus. $Q=K_{\alpha}+K_{D}$ Kinetic energy can be expressed in terms of momentum (p) and mass (m) as $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ . Since $p_{\alpha}=p_{D}$ , we have : $K_{D}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{D}}$ and $K_{\alpha}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}$ Therefore, $\frac{K_{D}}{K_{\alpha}}=\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}}$ . Substituting $K_{D}=K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})$ into the Q -value equation: $Q=K_{\alpha}+K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})=K_{\alpha}(1+\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})=K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{D}+m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})$ Since $m_{D}+m_{\alpha} \approx A$ (mass number of parent) and $m_{D} \approx A-4$ : $K_{\alpha}=Q(\frac{A-4}{A})$ The Q-value is the same ( 1 MeV ) for both substances. For Substance A ( $A_{A}=200$ ) : $K_{\alpha A}=Q(\frac{200-4}{200})=Q(\frac{196}{200})$ For Substance $B(A_{B}=212)$ : $K_{\alpha B}=Q(\frac{212-4}{212})=Q(\frac{208}{212})$ So, the ratio is; $\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}}=\frac{Q(\frac{196}{200})}{Q(\frac{208}{212})}=\frac{196}{200} \times \frac{212}{208}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}}=\frac{49}{50} \times \frac{53}{52}=\frac{49 \times 53}{50 \times 52}=\frac{2597}{2600}$ Therefore, the ratio of energies of $\alpha$ -rays produced by A and B is $\frac{2597}{2600}$ . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
In $\alpha$ -decay, a parent nucleus (X) of mass number A decays into a daughter nucleus (Y) and an $\alpha$ -particle (Helium nucleus, mass number 4).

$X_{Z}^{A} \rightarrow Y_{Z-2}^{A-4}+He_{2}^{4}$

Using conservation of momentum, the momentum of the $\alpha$ -particle ( $p_{\alpha}$ ) must be equal and opposite to the momentum of the daughter nucleus $(p_{D})$ .

And using energy balance ( Q -value) the total kinetic energy released ( Q ) is shared between the $\alpha$ -particle and the daughter nucleus.

$Q=K_{\alpha}+K_{D}$

Kinetic energy can be expressed in terms of momentum (p) and mass (m) as $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ .

Since $p_{\alpha}=p_{D}$ , we have :

$K_{D}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{D}}$ and $K_{\alpha}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}$

Therefore, $\frac{K_{D}}{K_{\alpha}}=\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}}$ .

Substituting $K_{D}=K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})$ into the Q -value equation:

$Q=K_{\alpha}+K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})=K_{\alpha}(1+\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})=K_{\alpha}(\frac{m_{D}+m_{\alpha}}{m_{D}})$

Since $m_{D}+m_{\alpha} \approx A$ (mass number of parent) and $m_{D} \approx A-4$ :

$K_{\alpha}=Q(\frac{A-4}{A})$

The Q-value is the same ( 1 MeV ) for both substances.

For Substance A ( $A_{A}=200$ ) :

$K_{\alpha A}=Q(\frac{200-4}{200})=Q(\frac{196}{200})$

For Substance $B(A_{B}=212)$ :

$K_{\alpha B}=Q(\frac{212-4}{212})=Q(\frac{208}{212})$

So, the ratio is;

$\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}}=\frac{Q(\frac{196}{200})}{Q(\frac{208}{212})}=\frac{196}{200} \times \frac{212}{208}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}}=\frac{49}{50} \times \frac{53}{52}=\frac{49 \times 53}{50 \times 52}=\frac{2597}{2600}$

Therefore, the ratio of energies of $\alpha$ -rays produced by A and B is $\frac{2597}{2600}$ .

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: In the hydrogen atom, the electron makes a transition from the higher orbit (i) to a lower orbit $(f)$ . The ratio of the radius of the orbits in given by $r_{i}:r_{f}=16:4$ . The wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is $____$ nm. (Given Rydberg constant $=1.0973 \times 10^{7}/m$ )
questions.question_html:
In the hydrogen atom, the electron makes a transition from the higher orbit (i) to a lower orbit $(f)$ . The ratio of the radius of the orbits in given by $r_{i}:r_{f}=16:4$ . The wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is $____$ nm.

(Given Rydberg constant $=1.0973 \times 10^{7}/m$ )
questions.explanation_text: The radius of an electron in the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by the formula: $r_{n}=(\frac{\epsilon_{0}ℎ^{2}}{\pi me^{2}})n^{2} \Rightarrow r_{n}∝n^{2}$ The ratio of radii of $i^{\text{th}}$ orbit to $f^{\text{th}}$ orbit is $r_{i}:r_{f}=16:4$ , $\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{n_{f}^{2}}=\frac{16}{4}=4$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{n_{i}}{n_{f}}=2 \Rightarrow n_{i}=2n_{f}$ For a transition to a lower orbit in a hydrogen atom, the simplest integers satisfying this are $n_{f}=2$ and $n_{i}=$ 4. The wavelength of the emitted photon is given by the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{n_{f}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{i}^{2}})$ Substituting the values $n_{f}=2$ and $n_{i}=4$ : $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{4-1}{16})=\frac{3R}{16}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{16}{3R}$ Putting the value of Rydberg's constant $R=1.0973 \times 10^{7}m^{-1}$ $\lambda=\frac{16}{3 \times 1.0973 \times 10^{7}} \approx 4.86 \times 10^{-7}m=486 \times 10^{-9}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=486nm$ Therefore, the wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is 486 nm . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
The radius of an electron in the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by the formula:

$r_{n}=(\frac{\epsilon_{0}ℎ^{2}}{\pi me^{2}})n^{2} \Rightarrow r_{n}∝n^{2}$

The ratio of radii of $i^{\text{th}}$ orbit to $f^{\text{th}}$ orbit is $r_{i}:r_{f}=16:4$ ,

$\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{n_{f}^{2}}=\frac{16}{4}=4$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{n_{i}}{n_{f}}=2 \Rightarrow n_{i}=2n_{f}$

For a transition to a lower orbit in a hydrogen atom, the simplest integers satisfying this are $n_{f}=2$ and $n_{i}=$ 4.

The wavelength of the emitted photon is given by the Rydberg formula:

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{n_{f}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{i}^{2}})$

Substituting the values $n_{f}=2$ and $n_{i}=4$ :

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})=R(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{4-1}{16})=\frac{3R}{16}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{16}{3R}$

Putting the value of Rydberg's constant $R=1.0973 \times 10^{7}m^{-1}$

$\lambda=\frac{16}{3 \times 1.0973 \times 10^{7}} \approx 4.86 \times 10^{-7}m=486 \times 10^{-9}m$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=486nm$

Therefore, the wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is 486 nm .

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: The smallest wavelength of Lyman series is 91 nm . The difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly $____$ nm.
questions.question_html: The smallest wavelength of Lyman series is 91 nm . The difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly $____$ nm.
questions.explanation_text: The energy of $n^{\text{th}}$ energy state of hydrogen atom is $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}$ The wavelengths of the spectral lines of hydrogen-like atoms are governed by the Rydberg formula $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$ Where : $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the emitted photon. R is the Rydberg constant. $n_{1}$ is the principal quantum number of the lower energy level. $n_{2}$ is the principal quantum number of the higher energy level ( $n_{2}>n_{1}$ ). The smallest wavelength corresponds to the highest energy transition (from $n_{2}=\infty$ to $n_{1}$ ). The largest wavelength corresponds to the lowest energy transition (from the immediate next energy level, $n_{2}=n_{1}+1$ , down to $n_{1}$ ). For the Lyman series, the electron transitions fall to the ground state, so $n_{1}=1$ . The smallest wavelength $(\lambda_{L(min)})$ occurs when $n_{2}=\infty$ . It is given that $\lambda_{L,min}=91nm$ . Using the Rydberg formula : $\frac{1}{\lambda_{L,min}}=R(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{91}=R(1-0) \Rightarrow R=\frac{1}{91}nm^{-1}$ For the Balmer series, the lower energy level is $n_{1}=2$ . The largest wavelength ( $\lambda_{B,max}$ corresponds to the smallest energy jump, which is from $n_{2}=3$ to $n_{1}=2$ . Applying the formula : $\frac{1}{\lambda_{B,max}}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}})=R(\frac{5}{36})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{B,max}}=\frac{1}{91} \times \frac{5}{36}nm^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda_{B,max}=\frac{91 \times 36}{5}nm=655.2nm$ For the Paschen series, the lower energy level is $n_{1}=3$ . The largest wavelength ( $\lambda_{P,max}$ ) corresponds to the smallest energy jump, which is from $n_{2}=4$ to $n_{1}=3$ . Applying the formula : $\frac{1}{\lambda_{P,max}}=R(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})=R(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{P,max}}=\frac{1}{91} \times \frac{7}{144}nm^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda_{P,max}=\frac{91 \times 144}{7}nm=1871nm$ So, the difference between these two largest wavelengths : $\Delta\lambda=\lambda_{P,max}-\lambda_{B,max}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta\lambda=1872nm-655.2nm$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta\lambda=1216.8nm \approx 1217nm$ Therefore, the difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly 1217 nm. Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
The energy of $n^{\text{th}}$ energy state of hydrogen atom is $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}$

The wavelengths of the spectral lines of hydrogen-like atoms are governed by the Rydberg formula

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$

Where :

  • $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the emitted photon.

  • R is the Rydberg constant.

  • $n_{1}$ is the principal quantum number of the lower energy level.

  • $n_{2}$ is the principal quantum number of the higher energy level ( $n_{2}>n_{1}$ ).

The smallest wavelength corresponds to the highest energy transition (from $n_{2}=\infty$ to $n_{1}$ ).

The largest wavelength corresponds to the lowest energy transition (from the immediate next energy level, $n_{2}=n_{1}+1$ , down to $n_{1}$ ).

For the Lyman series, the electron transitions fall to the ground state, so $n_{1}=1$ . The smallest wavelength $(\lambda_{L(min)})$ occurs when $n_{2}=\infty$ .

It is given that $\lambda_{L,min}=91nm$ .

Using the Rydberg formula :

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{L,min}}=R(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{91}=R(1-0) \Rightarrow R=\frac{1}{91}nm^{-1}$

For the Balmer series, the lower energy level is $n_{1}=2$ .

The largest wavelength ( $\lambda_{B,max}$ corresponds to the smallest energy jump, which is from $n_{2}=3$ to $n_{1}=2$ .

Applying the formula :

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{B,max}}=R(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}})=R(\frac{5}{36})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{B,max}}=\frac{1}{91} \times \frac{5}{36}nm^{-1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda_{B,max}=\frac{91 \times 36}{5}nm=655.2nm$

For the Paschen series, the lower energy level is $n_{1}=3$ .

The largest wavelength ( $\lambda_{P,max}$ ) corresponds to the smallest energy jump, which is from $n_{2}=4$ to $n_{1}=3$ .

Applying the formula :

$\frac{1}{\lambda_{P,max}}=R(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})=R(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{P,max}}=\frac{1}{91} \times \frac{7}{144}nm^{-1}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda_{P,max}=\frac{91 \times 144}{7}nm=1871nm$

So, the difference between these two largest wavelengths :

$\Delta\lambda=\lambda_{P,max}-\lambda_{B,max}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta\lambda=1872nm-655.2nm$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta\lambda=1216.8nm \approx 1217nm$

Therefore, the difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly 1217 nm.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.explanation_text: The binding energy (B.E.) of a nucleus is the energy required to disassemble it into its constituent nucleons. Total B.E. $=($ Binding Energy per nucleon $) \times ($ Number of nucleons A $)$ Energy Released (Q) = (Total B.E. of Products) - (Total B.E. of Reactants) The given reaction is $H_{1}^{2}+H_{1}^{2} \rightarrow He_{2}^{4}$ The reactants are two nuclei of $H_{1}^{2}$ . B.E. per nucleon of $H_{1}^{2}=1.1MeV$ Number of nucleons (A) for one $H_{1}^{2}=2$ So, total B.E. of reactants $=2 \times (1.1 \times 2)=4.4MeV$ The product is one nucleus of $He_{2}^{4}$ . B.E. per nucleon of $He_{2}^{4}=7.2MeV$ Number of nucleons (A) for $He_{2}^{4}=4$ So, total B.E. of product $=7.2 \times 4=28.8MeV$ Hence, energy released during reaction is, $Q=28.8MeV-4.4MeV$ $\Rightarrow$ $Q=24.4MeV$ Therefore, the energy released if hydrogen atoms are combined to form $He_{2}^{4}$ is 24.4 MeV . The binding energy (B.E.) of a nucleus is the energy required to disassemble it into its constituent nucleons.

Total B.E. $=($ Binding Energy per nucleon $) \times ($ Number of nucleons A $)$

Energy Released (Q) = (Total B.E. of Products) - (Total B.E. of Reactants)

The given reaction is $H_{1}^{2}+H_{1}^{2} \rightarrow He_{2}^{4}$

The reactants are two nuclei of $H_{1}^{2}$ .

B.E. per nucleon of $H_{1}^{2}=1.1MeV$

Number of nucleons (A) for one $H_{1}^{2}=2$

So, total B.E. of reactants $=2 \times (1.1 \times 2)=4.4MeV$

The product is one nucleus of $He_{2}^{4}$ .

B.E. per nucleon of $He_{2}^{4}=7.2MeV$

Number of nucleons (A) for $He_{2}^{4}=4$

Hence, energy released during reaction is,

$Q=28.8MeV-4.4MeV$

Therefore, the energy released if hydrogen atoms are combined to form $He_{2}^{4}$ is 24.4 MeV .

questions.explanation_text: In the experiment, alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei) are fired at a thin gold foil. Rutherford observed that most particles passed straight through, but a tiny fraction (about 1 in 8000 ) reflected back at angles greater than $90^{\circ}$ . Statement A: Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus. Since the nucleus is tiny compared to the total volume of the atom, the probability of an alpha particle hitting it or coming close enough to be repelled backward is very low. Hence, statement A is true. Statement B: Alpha particles have a charge of +2 e , while a gold nucleus has a charge of +79 e . They do not have equal charges. Hence, statement B is false. Statement C: The impact parameter (b) is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the alpha particle from the centre of the nucleus. A rebound or large-angle scattering occurs when the impact parameter is very small (close to zero), meaning the particle is heading almost directly toward the nucleus. Only a few particles have such a small impact parameter. Hence, the statement C is true. Statement D: The kinetic energy of the incident alpha particles is generally uniform in the beam; high kinetic energy would actually make it easier to penetrate closer to the nucleus rather than causing the few rebounds mentioned. Hence, the statement D is false. Statement E: A head-on collision occurs when the particle moves directly toward the centre of the nucleus $(b=0)$ . Because the nucleus is so small, only a very small number of particles are aligned for such a collision. Hence, the statement E is true. Therefore, statements A, C, and E are the correct reasons for the observed phenomenon. Thus, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
In the experiment, alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei) are fired at a thin gold foil. Rutherford observed that most particles passed straight through, but a tiny fraction (about 1 in 8000 ) reflected back at angles greater than $90^{\circ}$ .

Statement A: Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus. Since the nucleus is tiny compared to the total volume of the atom, the probability of an alpha particle hitting it or coming close enough to be repelled backward is very low.

Hence, statement A is true.

Statement B: Alpha particles have a charge of +2 e , while a gold nucleus has a charge of +79 e . They do not have equal charges. Hence, statement B is false.

Statement C: The impact parameter (b) is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the alpha particle from the centre of the nucleus.

A rebound or large-angle scattering occurs when the impact parameter is very small (close to zero), meaning the particle is heading almost directly toward the nucleus. Only a few particles have such a small impact parameter. Hence, the statement C is true.

Statement D: The kinetic energy of the incident alpha particles is generally uniform in the beam; high kinetic energy would actually make it easier to penetrate closer to the nucleus rather than causing the few rebounds mentioned. Hence, the statement D is false.

Statement E: A head-on collision occurs when the particle moves directly toward the centre of the nucleus $(b=0)$ . Because the nucleus is so small, only a very small number of particles are aligned for such a collision. Hence, the statement E is true.

Therefore, statements A, C, and E are the correct reasons for the observed phenomenon.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: The minimum frequency of photon required to break a particle of mass 15.348 amu into $4\alpha$ particles is $____$ kHz . [mass of He nucleus = $4.002amu,1amu=1.66 \times 10^{-27}kg,h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ and $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ ]
questions.question_html:
The minimum frequency of photon required to break a particle of mass 15.348 amu into $4\alpha$ particles is $____$ kHz .

[mass of He nucleus = $4.002amu,1amu=1.66 \times 10^{-27}kg,h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ and $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ ]
questions.explanation_text: Einstein's equation tells us that mass and energy are interchangeable. $E=mc^{2}$ When a nuclear reaction occurs, the total mass of the products is often slightly different from the initial mass of the reactants. If the products are lighter, the missing mass is released as energy. If the products are heavier, energy must be supplied to create that extra mass. It is given that a particle breaks into $4\alpha$ particles. Initial mass of the single particle. $M_{\text{initial}}=15.348amu$ Final mass of $4\alpha$ particles $=M_{\text{final}}=4 \times$ mass of He nucleus $M_{final}=4 \times 4.002amu=16.008amu$ The mass defect ( $\Delta m$ ) during this nuclear reaction is, $\Delta m=M_{\text{final}}-M_{\text{initial}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=16.008amu-15.348amu$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=0.66amu$ It is given that $1amu=1.66 \times 10^{-27}kg$ . $\Delta m=0.66 \times (1.66 \times 10^{-27})kg$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=1.0956 \times 10^{-27}kg$ Now using Einstein's equation, $E=\Delta m \cdot c^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.0956 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.0956 \times 10^{-27}) \times (9 \times 10^{16})$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=9.8604 \times 10^{-11}\text{Joules}$ This energy is provided by a single photon. The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency ( $v$ ), given by Planck's equation: $E=h\nu$ Where h is Planck's constant $(6.6 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s)$ . $v=\frac{E}{ℎ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v=\frac{9.8604 \times 10^{-11}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v=1.494 \times 10^{23}Hz$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{kHz}=1.494 \times 10^{23} \times 10^{-3}kHz$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{kHz}=14.94 \times 10^{19}kHz$ Therefore, the minimum frequency of photon required is $14.94 \times 10^{19}kHz$ . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Einstein's equation tells us that mass and energy are interchangeable.

$E=mc^{2}$

When a nuclear reaction occurs, the total mass of the products is often slightly different from the initial mass of the reactants.

  • If the products are lighter, the missing mass is released as energy.

  • If the products are heavier, energy must be supplied to create that extra mass.

It is given that a particle breaks into $4\alpha$ particles.

Initial mass of the single particle. $M_{\text{initial}}=15.348amu$

Final mass of $4\alpha$ particles $=M_{\text{final}}=4 \times$ mass of He nucleus

$M_{final}=4 \times 4.002amu=16.008amu$

The mass defect ( $\Delta m$ ) during this nuclear reaction is,

$\Delta m=M_{\text{final}}-M_{\text{initial}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=16.008amu-15.348amu$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=0.66amu$

It is given that $1amu=1.66 \times 10^{-27}kg$ .

$\Delta m=0.66 \times (1.66 \times 10^{-27})kg$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta m=1.0956 \times 10^{-27}kg$

Now using Einstein's equation,

$E=\Delta m \cdot c^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.0956 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=(1.0956 \times 10^{-27}) \times (9 \times 10^{16})$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=9.8604 \times 10^{-11}\text{Joules}$

This energy is provided by a single photon. The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency ( $v$ ), given by Planck's equation:

$E=h\nu$

Where h is Planck's constant $(6.6 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s)$ .

$v=\frac{E}{ℎ}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v=\frac{9.8604 \times 10^{-11}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v=1.494 \times 10^{23}Hz$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{kHz}=1.494 \times 10^{23} \times 10^{-3}kHz$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{kHz}=14.94 \times 10^{19}kHz$

Therefore, the minimum frequency of photon required is $14.94 \times 10^{19}kHz$ .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.explanation_text: To evaluate the assertion and reason provided, we need to consider the formula for the density of a nucleus. The density $\rho$ can be expressed as follows: $\rho=\frac{M}{V}=\frac{m_{n} \times A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}$ Here, $m_{n}$ represents the nucleon mass, $A$ is the mass number, and $R$ is the radius of the nucleus. According to the formula for the radius: $R=R_{0}A^{1/3}$ This indicates that the radius $R$ is proportional to $A^{1/3}$ . By substituting the expression for $R$ in terms of $A$ back into the formula for density, we get: $\rho=\frac{m_{n} \times A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi(A^{1/3}R_{0})^{3}}$ Simplifying the equation shows that the $A$ terms cancel out: $\rho=\frac{m_{n}}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_{0}^{3}}$ This reveals that the nuclear density $\rho$ is approximately constant and independent of the mass number $A$ . Therefore, the densities of copper $(_{29}^{64}\text{Cu})$ and carbon $(_{6}^{12}\text{C})$ nuclei are effectively the same because the density formula results in a similar value regardless of the specific mass number.

Energy released when two deuterons $(_{1}H^{2})$ fuse to form a helium nucleus $(_{2}He^{4})$ is :
(Given : Binding energy per nucleon of $_{1}H^{2}=1.1MeV$ and binding energy per nucleon of $_{2}He^{4}=7.0MeV$ )
questions.question_html: Energy released when two deuterons $(_{1}H^{2})$ fuse to form a helium nucleus $(_{2}He^{4})$ is : (Given : Binding energy per nucleon of $_{1}H^{2}=1.1MeV$ and binding energy per nucleon of $_{2}He^{4}=7.0MeV$ )
questions.explanation_text: To calculate the energy released when two deuterons ( $_{1}H^{2}$ ) fuse to form a helium nucleus ( $_{2}He^{4}$ ), consider the following: The reaction is represented as: $_{1}H^{2}+_{1}H^{2} \rightarrow _{2}He^{4}$ Given the binding energy per nucleon: For $_{1}H^{2}$ : 1.1 MeV For $_{2}He^{4}$ : 7.0 MeV Calculating Binding Energy Binding Energy for Reactants : Each deuteron ( $_{1}H^{2}$ ) has a binding energy of $1.1\text{MeV}$ per nucleon. Since there are two nucleons in a deuteron, the total binding energy for one deuteron is $1.1 \times 2=2.2\text{MeV}$ . Therefore, for two deuterons: $2.2 \times 2=4.4\text{MeV}$ . Binding Energy for Product : For $_{2}He^{4}$ : Each of the four nucleons has a binding energy of $7.0\text{MeV}$ . Total binding energy for the helium nucleus: $7.0 \times 4=28.0\text{MeV}$ . Energy Released (Q) The energy released, $Q$ , is the difference between the binding energy of the products and the reactants: $Q=BE_{\text{product}}-BE_{\text{reactants}}=28.0\text{MeV}-4.4\text{MeV}=23.6\text{MeV}$ Thus, the energy released when two deuterons fuse to form a helium nucleus is 23.6 MeV .
questions.explanation_html:
To calculate the energy released when two deuterons ( $_{1}H^{2}$ ) fuse to form a helium nucleus ( $_{2}He^{4}$ ), consider the following:

The reaction is represented as:

$_{1}H^{2}+_{1}H^{2} \rightarrow _{2}He^{4}$

Given the binding energy per nucleon:

For $_{1}H^{2}$ : 1.1 MeV

For $_{2}He^{4}$ : 7.0 MeV

Calculating Binding Energy

Binding Energy for Reactants:

Each deuteron ( $_{1}H^{2}$ ) has a binding energy of $1.1\text{MeV}$ per nucleon.

Since there are two nucleons in a deuteron, the total binding energy for one deuteron is $1.1 \times 2=2.2\text{MeV}$ .

Therefore, for two deuterons: $2.2 \times 2=4.4\text{MeV}$ .

Binding Energy for Product:

For $_{2}He^{4}$ : Each of the four nucleons has a binding energy of $7.0\text{MeV}$ .

Total binding energy for the helium nucleus: $7.0 \times 4=28.0\text{MeV}$ .

Energy Released (Q)

The energy released, $Q$ , is the difference between the binding energy of the products and the reactants:

$Q=BE_{\text{product}}-BE_{\text{reactants}}=28.0\text{MeV}-4.4\text{MeV}=23.6\text{MeV}$

Thus, the energy released when two deuterons fuse to form a helium nucleus is 23.6 MeV.

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze both statements: Assertion (A): “The binding energy per nucleon is found to be practically independent of the atomic number A, for nuclei with mass numbers between 30 and 170.” In fact, for nuclei in this mass range, the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant (around 7–8 MeV per nucleon). This is because the attractive nuclear force saturates, leading to a relatively uniform binding energy per nucleon in medium to heavy nuclei. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true. Reason (R): “Nuclear force is long range.” The nuclear force (or strong force) that holds the nucleons (protons and neutrons) together is actually very short-ranged. Its effective range is approximately 1 to 3 femtometers (fm), after which the force rapidly decreases. Hence, Reason (R) is false. Since the assertion is correct and the reason is incorrect, the correct answer is: Option A: (A) is true but (R) is false.

Assertion (A): “The binding energy per nucleon is found to be practically independent of the atomic number A, for nuclei with mass numbers between 30 and 170.”

In fact, for nuclei in this mass range, the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant (around 7–8 MeV per nucleon). This is because the attractive nuclear force saturates, leading to a relatively uniform binding energy per nucleon in medium to heavy nuclei.

Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R): “Nuclear force is long range.”

The nuclear force (or strong force) that holds the nucleons (protons and neutrons) together is actually very short-ranged. Its effective range is approximately 1 to 3 femtometers (fm), after which the force rapidly decreases.

Hence, Reason (R) is false.

Since the assertion is correct and the reason is incorrect, the correct answer is:

Option A: (A) is true but (R) is false.

questions.question_html: In a hydrogen like ion, the energy difference between the $2^{\text{nd}}$ excitation energy state and ground is 108.8 eV . The atomic number of the ion is:
questions.explanation_text: To determine the atomic number (Z) of a hydrogen-like ion, given that the energy difference between its second excitation state and the ground state is 108.8 eV, we use the following formula for the energy difference between two energy levels in a hydrogen-like atom: $\Delta E=13.6\text{eV} \times Z^{2}[\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}]$ Here, for the second excitation, $n_{2}=3$ (since excitation means moving to the second higher energy level beyond the ground state, which means $n_{1}=1$ for the ground state to $n_{2}=3$ ). Plug these into the energy difference formula: $\Delta E=13.6Z^{2}[\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}]$ Simplifying the term in brackets: $\Delta E=13.6Z^{2}[1-\frac{1}{9}]=13.6Z^{2} \times \frac{8}{9}$ Given that $\Delta E=108.8\text{eV}$ , set the equations equal: $13.6\frac{8Z^{2}}{9}=108.8$ Solving for $Z$ , first simplify: $13.6 \times \frac{8}{9} \times Z^{2}=108.8$ $\frac{108.8 \times 9}{13.6 \times 8}=Z^{2}$ $Z^{2}=9$ Thus, the atomic number $Z$ is: $Z=3$ The atomic number of the ion is 3.

$\Delta E=13.6\text{eV} \times Z^{2}[\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}]$

Here, for the second excitation, $n_{2}=3$ (since excitation means moving to the second higher energy level beyond the ground state, which means $n_{1}=1$ for the ground state to $n_{2}=3$ ). Plug these into the energy difference formula:

$\Delta E=13.6Z^{2}[\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}]$

Simplifying the term in brackets:

$\Delta E=13.6Z^{2}[1-\frac{1}{9}]=13.6Z^{2} \times \frac{8}{9}$

Given that $\Delta E=108.8\text{eV}$ , set the equations equal:

$13.6\frac{8Z^{2}}{9}=108.8$

Solving for $Z$ , first simplify:

$13.6 \times \frac{8}{9} \times Z^{2}=108.8$

$\frac{108.8 \times 9}{13.6 \times 8}=Z^{2}$

$Z^{2}=9$

Thus, the atomic number $Z$ is:

$Z=3$

The atomic number of the ion is 3.

questions.question_text: A radioactive nucleus $n_{2}$ has 3 times the decay constant as compared to the decay constant of another radioactive nucleus $n_{1}$ . If initial number of both nuclei are the same, what is the ratio of number of nuclei of $n_{2}$ to the number of nuclei of $n_{1}$ , after one half-life of $n_{1}$ ?
questions.question_html: A radioactive nucleus $n_{2}$ has 3 times the decay constant as compared to the decay constant of another radioactive nucleus $n_{1}$ . If initial number of both nuclei are the same, what is the ratio of number of nuclei of $n_{2}$ to the number of nuclei of $n_{1}$ , after one half-life of $n_{1}$ ?
questions.explanation_text: Let's work through the problem step by step. The decay of a radioactive nucleus is given by the formula: $N(t)=N_{0}e^{-\lambda t},$ where: $N(t)$ is the number of nuclei remaining at time $t$ , $N_{0}$ is the initial number of nuclei, $\lambda$ is the decay constant. For nucleus $n_{1}$ with decay constant $\lambda_{1}$ , its half-life $t_{1/2}$ is: $t_{1/2}=\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}.$ After one half-life of $n_{1}$ , the number of $n_{1}$ nuclei remaining is: $N_{1}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{1}t_{1/2}}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{1}\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}}=N_{0}e^{-ln2}=\frac{N_{0}}{2}.$ Nucleus $n_{2}$ has a decay constant that is 3 times that of $n_{1}$ : $\lambda_{2}=3\lambda_{1}.$ For nucleus $n_{2}$ , the number of nuclei remaining after one half-life of $n_{1}$ (which is $t=\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}$ ) is: $N_{2}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{2}t}=N_{0}e^{-3\lambda_{1}\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}}=N_{0}e^{-3ln2}=N_{0} \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}=\frac{N_{0}}{8}.$ Now, we find the ratio of $n_{2}$ nuclei to $n_{1}$ nuclei after this time: $\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=\frac{\frac{N_{0}}{8}}{\frac{N_{0}}{2}}=\frac{1/8}{1/2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, the correct ratio is $\frac{1}{4}$ , which corresponds to Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's work through the problem step by step.

The decay of a radioactive nucleus is given by the formula:

$N(t)=N_{0}e^{-\lambda t},$

where:

$N(t)$ is the number of nuclei remaining at time $t$ ,

$N_{0}$ is the initial number of nuclei,

$\lambda$ is the decay constant.

For nucleus $n_{1}$ with decay constant $\lambda_{1}$ , its half-life $t_{1/2}$ is:

$t_{1/2}=\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}.$

After one half-life of $n_{1}$ , the number of $n_{1}$ nuclei remaining is:

$N_{1}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{1}t_{1/2}}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{1}\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}}=N_{0}e^{-ln2}=\frac{N_{0}}{2}.$

Nucleus $n_{2}$ has a decay constant that is 3 times that of $n_{1}$ :

$\lambda_{2}=3\lambda_{1}.$

For nucleus $n_{2}$ , the number of nuclei remaining after one half-life of $n_{1}$ (which is $t=\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}$ ) is:

$N_{2}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda_{2}t}=N_{0}e^{-3\lambda_{1}\frac{ln2}{\lambda_{1}}}=N_{0}e^{-3ln2}=N_{0} \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}=\frac{N_{0}}{8}.$

Now, we find the ratio of $n_{2}$ nuclei to $n_{1}$ nuclei after this time:

$\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=\frac{\frac{N_{0}}{8}}{\frac{N_{0}}{2}}=\frac{1/8}{1/2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

Therefore, the correct ratio is $\frac{1}{4}$ , which corresponds to Option A.

questions.question_text: An electron in the hydrogen atom initially in the fourth excited state makes a transition to $n^{\text{th}}$ energy state by emitting a photon of energy 2.86 eV . The integer value of n will be__________.
questions.question_html: An electron in the hydrogen atom initially in the fourth excited state makes a transition to $n^{\text{th}}$ energy state by emitting a photon of energy 2.86 eV . The integer value of n will be__________.
questions.explanation_text: To find the integer value of $n$ for which an electron transitions from the fourth excited state in a hydrogen atom, thus emitting a photon with an energy of 2.86 eV, we can follow these steps: We use the formula for the energy difference associated with electron transitions in a hydrogen atom: $E=13.6(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$ However, in this question, it seems there's a typo in the original explanation, as both indices are given as $n_{1}$ . To correct it, we should use this formula: $E=13.6(\frac{1}{n^{2}}-\frac{1}{5^{2}})$ where $n_{1}=5$ (the fifth energy level or fourth excited state) and $n_{2}=n$ (the state to which the electron transitions). Given the photon's energy is 2.86 eV, set up the equation: $2.86=13.6(\frac{1}{n^{2}}-\frac{1}{25})$ Solve for $\frac{1}{n^{2}}$ : $\frac{1}{n^{2}}=\frac{2.86}{13.6}+\frac{1}{25}$ Calculate the value: $\frac{1}{n^{2}}=0.21+0.04=0.25$ Find $n^{2}$ : $n^{2}=\frac{1}{0.25}=4$ Consequently: $n=\sqrt{4}=2$ Thus, the electron transitions to the $n=2$ energy state.

$n^{2}=\frac{1}{0.25}=4$

Consequently:

$n=\sqrt{4}=2$

Thus, the electron transitions to the $n=2$ energy state.

questions.explanation_text: In Bohr's atomic model, the energy of an electron in an atom is given by the formula: $E∝\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}$ where $Z$ is the atomic number and $n$ is the principal quantum number of the electron's orbit. Let’s consider the implications: For hydrogen ( $H$ ), $Z=1$ . For helium ion ( $He^{+}$ ), $Z=2$ . For lithium ion ( $Li^{++}$ ), $Z=3$ . Helium Ion ( $He^{+}$ ) in the First Excited State : $E∝\frac{2^{2}}{2^{2}}=1$ This matches the energy of hydrogen in its ground state. Lithium Ion ( $Li^{++}$ ) in the Second Excited State : $E∝\frac{3^{2}}{3^{2}}=1$ This also matches the energy of hydrogen in its ground state. From this analysis, we can conclude: The energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is equal to the energy of a $He^{+}$ ion in its first excited state. The energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state also equals the energy of a $Li^{++}$ ion in its second excited state. Hence, statements (A) and (B) are correct.

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom in ground state is given an energy of $10.2eV$ . How many spectral lines will be emitted due to transition of electrons?
questions.question_html: A hydrogen atom in ground state is given an energy of $10.2eV$ . How many spectral lines will be emitted due to transition of electrons?
questions.explanation_text: To determine how many spectral lines will be emitted due to transitions of electrons in a hydrogen atom when it is given an energy of $10.2\text{eV}$ , we first need to ascertain which energy level the electron will reach with this energy and then count the possible transitions (spectral lines) as it returns to the ground state. Energy Levels of Hydrogen Atom : The energy levels $E_{n}$ of a hydrogen atom can be calculated using the formula: $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{n^{2}}$ where $n$ is the principal quantum number. Ground State Energy : The ground state (n=1) energy is $E_{1}=-13.6\text{eV}$ . Determine the Excited State : If the ground state electron is given $10.2\text{eV}$ , its total energy becomes: $E_{\text{total}}=E_{1}+10.2\text{eV}=-13.6\text{eV}+10.2\text{eV}=-3.4\text{eV}$ Now, we find the principal quantum number $n$ for which the energy is closest to $-3.4\text{eV}$ : For $n=2$ : $E_{2}=-\frac{13.6}{2^{2}}=-3.4\text{eV}$ For $n=3$ : $E_{3}=-\frac{13.6}{3^{2}}=-1.51\text{eV}$ Since $-3.4\text{eV}$ matches exactly with $E_{2}$ , the electron reaches the second energy level ( $n=2$ ). Counting Spectral Lines : When the electron falls back to the ground state from $n=2$ , it can do so in a single transition: $n=2$ to $n=1$ Thus, only one spectral line will be emitted during this transition. Conclusion : The number of spectral lines emitted when a hydrogen atom in the ground state is given $10.2\text{eV}$ and the electron transitions back to the ground state from $n=2$ is just one. Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D: 1 .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine how many spectral lines will be emitted due to transitions of electrons in a hydrogen atom when it is given an energy of $10.2\text{eV}$ , we first need to ascertain which energy level the electron will reach with this energy and then count the possible transitions (spectral lines) as it returns to the ground state.

Energy Levels of Hydrogen Atom :

The energy levels $E_{n}$ of a hydrogen atom can be calculated using the formula:

$E_{n}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{n^{2}}$

where $n$ is the principal quantum number.

Ground State Energy :

The ground state (n=1) energy is $E_{1}=-13.6\text{eV}$ .

Determine the Excited State :

If the ground state electron is given $10.2\text{eV}$ , its total energy becomes:

$E_{\text{total}}=E_{1}+10.2\text{eV}=-13.6\text{eV}+10.2\text{eV}=-3.4\text{eV}$

Now, we find the principal quantum number $n$ for which the energy is closest to $-3.4\text{eV}$ :

  • For $n=2$ : $E_{2}=-\frac{13.6}{2^{2}}=-3.4\text{eV}$

  • For $n=3$ : $E_{3}=-\frac{13.6}{3^{2}}=-1.51\text{eV}$

Since $-3.4\text{eV}$ matches exactly with $E_{2}$ , the electron reaches the second energy level ( $n=2$ ).

Counting Spectral Lines :

When the electron falls back to the ground state from $n=2$ , it can do so in a single transition:

  • $n=2$ to $n=1$

Thus, only one spectral line will be emitted during this transition.

Conclusion :

The number of spectral lines emitted when a hydrogen atom in the ground state is given $10.2\text{eV}$ and the electron transitions back to the ground state from $n=2$ is just one.

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option D: 1.

questions.question_text: Binding energy of a certain nucleus is $18 \times 10^{8}J$ . How much is the difference between total mass of all the nucleons and nuclear mass of the given nucleus:
questions.question_html: Binding energy of a certain nucleus is $18 \times 10^{8}J$ . How much is the difference between total mass of all the nucleons and nuclear mass of the given nucleus:
questions.explanation_text: To determine the difference between the total mass of all the nucleons and the nuclear mass of the given nucleus, we need to use the concept of mass-energy equivalence provided by Einstein's famous equation: $E=\Delta m \cdot c^{2}$ where: E is the binding energy. $\Delta m$ is the mass defect (difference in mass). $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, which is approximately $3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$ . Given: Binding energy, $E=18 \times 10^{8}\text{J}$ . We need to find $\Delta m$ , so rearranging the equation: $\Delta m=\frac{E}{c^{2}}$ Substitute the given values: $\Delta m=\frac{18 \times 10^{8}}{(3 \times 10^{8})^{2}}$ Calculate the value: $\Delta m=\frac{18 \times 10^{8}}{9 \times 10^{16}}$ $\Delta m=\frac{18}{9} \times 10^{-8}$ $\Delta m=2 \times 10^{-8}\text{kg}$ To convert the mass from kilograms to micrograms ( $\mu g$ ), we use the conversion factor $1\text{kg}=10^{9}\mu g$ : $\Delta m=2 \times 10^{-8}\text{kg} \times 10^{9}\frac{\mu g}{\text{kg}}$ $\Delta m=2 \times 10^{1}\mu g$ $\Delta m=20\mu g$ Therefore, the difference between the total mass of all the nucleons and the nuclear mass of the given nucleus is 20 $\mu g$ . Option A (20 $\mu g$ ) is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the difference between the total mass of all the nucleons and the nuclear mass of the given nucleus, we need to use the concept of mass-energy equivalence provided by Einstein's famous equation:

$E=\Delta m \cdot c^{2}$

where:

  • E is the binding energy.
  • $\Delta m$ is the mass defect (difference in mass).
  • $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, which is approximately $3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$ .

Given:

  • Binding energy, $E=18 \times 10^{8}\text{J}$ .

We need to find $\Delta m$ , so rearranging the equation:

$\Delta m=\frac{E}{c^{2}}$

Substitute the given values:

$\Delta m=\frac{18 \times 10^{8}}{(3 \times 10^{8})^{2}}$

Calculate the value:

$\Delta m=\frac{18 \times 10^{8}}{9 \times 10^{16}}$

$\Delta m=\frac{18}{9} \times 10^{-8}$

$\Delta m=2 \times 10^{-8}\text{kg}$

To convert the mass from kilograms to micrograms ( $\mu g$ ), we use the conversion factor $1\text{kg}=10^{9}\mu g$ :

$\Delta m=2 \times 10^{-8}\text{kg} \times 10^{9}\frac{\mu g}{\text{kg}}$

$\Delta m=2 \times 10^{1}\mu g$

$\Delta m=20\mu g$

Therefore, the difference between the total mass of all the nucleons and the nuclear mass of the given nucleus is 20 $\mu g$ .

Option A (20 $\mu g$ ) is the correct answer.

questions.question_text: An electron rotates in a circle around a nucleus having positive charge $Ze$ . Correct relation between total energy (E) of electron to its potential energy (U) is :
questions.question_html: An electron rotates in a circle around a nucleus having positive charge $Ze$ . Correct relation between total energy (E) of electron to its potential energy (U) is :
questions.explanation_text: In the context of an electron orbiting around a nucleus with a positive charge of $Ze$ , we are dealing with classical physics approximations and the electrostatic force between the electron and the nucleus. In such a setup, the electron's potential energy (U) is due to electrostatic interaction, and it is given by Coulomb's law: $U=-\frac{kZe^{2}}{r}$ Where: $U$ is the potential energy of the electron, $k$ is Coulomb's constant, $Z$ is the atomic number (number of protons in the nucleus), $e$ is the charge of an electron, and $r$ is the radius of the orbit of the electron around the nucleus. The negative sign indicates that the potential energy is negative because the electron and nucleus attract each other. The total energy (E) of the electron in orbit is the sum of its kinetic energy (K) and its potential energy (U). Since the electron is in a stable orbit, its kinetic energy can be shown to be exactly half the magnitude of its potential energy but positive: $K=-\frac{1}{2}U$ Therefore, $E=K+U=-\frac{1}{2}U+U=\frac{1}{2}U$ To find a relation between total energy (E) and potential energy (U), we rearrange the equation as follows: $2E=U$ This is to say, the total energy (E) is half the magnitude of potential energy (U) but negative, and the correct relationship between them, when looking for a positive proportionality, yields to $2E=U$ . Hence, the correct option is: Option C: $2E=U$

In such a setup, the electron's potential energy (U) is due to electrostatic interaction, and it is given by Coulomb's law:

$U=-\frac{kZe^{2}}{r}$

Where:

  • $U$ is the potential energy of the electron,
  • $k$ is Coulomb's constant,
  • $Z$ is the atomic number (number of protons in the nucleus),
  • $e$ is the charge of an electron, and
  • $r$ is the radius of the orbit of the electron around the nucleus.

The negative sign indicates that the potential energy is negative because the electron and nucleus attract each other.

The total energy (E) of the electron in orbit is the sum of its kinetic energy (K) and its potential energy (U). Since the electron is in a stable orbit, its kinetic energy can be shown to be exactly half the magnitude of its potential energy but positive:

$K=-\frac{1}{2}U$

Therefore,

$E=K+U=-\frac{1}{2}U+U=\frac{1}{2}U$

To find a relation between total energy (E) and potential energy (U), we rearrange the equation as follows:

$2E=U$

This is to say, the total energy (E) is half the magnitude of potential energy (U) but negative, and the correct relationship between them, when looking for a positive proportionality, yields to $2E=U$ . Hence, the correct option is:

Option C: $2E=U$

questions.question_text: The minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in ground state to emit radiation in Balmer series is nearly :
questions.question_html: The minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in ground state to emit radiation in Balmer series is nearly :
questions.explanation_text: The energy $E_{n}$ of an electron in the $n$ th energy level of a hydrogen atom is given by the formula: $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{n^{2}}$ where: $E_{n}$ is the energy in electron volts (eV), $13.6\text{eV}$ is the ionization energy of hydrogen (the energy required to remove the electron from the ground state, $n=1$ ), $n$ is the principal quantum number (an integer starting from 1). The Balmer Series The Balmer series is a specific set of spectral lines of hydrogen that are visible to the naked eye. It results from the electron making transitions between energy levels, specifically from levels with $n \ge 3$ (i.e., from higher energy states) down to $n=2$ . These transitions release energy in the form of electromagnetic radiation, which we observe as the Balmer series. Ground State Energy ( $E_{1}$ ): The energy of the electron in the ground state ( $n=1$ ) of hydrogen is: $E_{1}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{1^{2}}=-13.6\text{eV}$ This represents the electron's energy level when it's closest to the nucleus. Energy for the $n=3$ Level ( $E_{3}$ ): For an electron in the $n=3$ level, its energy is: $E_{3}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{3^{2}}=-1.51\text{eV}$ Minimum Energy for Balmer Series Transition: The minimum energy transition within the Balmer series is from $n=3$ to $n=2$ , but to understand the total energy required for an electron to emit radiation in the Balmer series, starting from the ground state, we consider the energy needed to first excite the electron from $n=1$ to $n=3$ . Energy Difference ( $\Delta E$ ): The energy emitted as radiation for the electron to transition from the ground state to a state where it can participate in the Balmer series is the difference between the ground state energy and the energy of the $n=3$ state: $\Delta E=E_{3}-E_{1}=-1.51\text{eV}-(-13.6\text{eV})=12.09\text{eV}$ Note This calculation shows that the minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in the ground state to emit radiation in the Balmer series is approximately 12.1 eV. The energy difference essentially represents the energy that must be supplied to an electron to excite it from the ground state ( $n=1$ ) to an excited state ( $n=3$ ) from which it can then transition to $n=2$ , emitting radiation observable as part of the Balmer series.

$E_{n}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{n^{2}}$

where:

  • $E_{n}$ is the energy in electron volts (eV),

  • $13.6\text{eV}$ is the ionization energy of hydrogen (the energy required to remove the electron from the ground state, $n=1$ ),

  • $n$ is the principal quantum number (an integer starting from 1).

The Balmer Series

The Balmer series is a specific set of spectral lines of hydrogen that are visible to the naked eye. It results from the electron making transitions between energy levels, specifically from levels with $n \ge 3$ (i.e., from higher energy states) down to $n=2$ . These transitions release energy in the form of electromagnetic radiation, which we observe as the Balmer series.

  1. Ground State Energy ( $E_{1}$ ): The energy of the electron in the ground state ( $n=1$ ) of hydrogen is:

$E_{1}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{1^{2}}=-13.6\text{eV}$

This represents the electron's energy level when it's closest to the nucleus.

  1. Energy for the $n=3$ Level ( $E_{3}$ ): For an electron in the $n=3$ level, its energy is:

$E_{3}=-\frac{13.6\text{eV}}{3^{2}}=-1.51\text{eV}$

  1. Minimum Energy for Balmer Series Transition: The minimum energy transition within the Balmer series is from $n=3$ to $n=2$ , but to understand the total energy required for an electron to emit radiation in the Balmer series, starting from the ground state, we consider the energy needed to first excite the electron from $n=1$ to $n=3$ .

  2. Energy Difference ( $\Delta E$ ): The energy emitted as radiation for the electron to transition from the ground state to a state where it can participate in the Balmer series is the difference between the ground state energy and the energy of the $n=3$ state:

$\Delta E=E_{3}-E_{1}=-1.51\text{eV}-(-13.6\text{eV})=12.09\text{eV}$

Note

This calculation shows that the minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in the ground state to emit radiation in the Balmer series is approximately 12.1 eV. The energy difference essentially represents the energy that must be supplied to an electron to excite it from the ground state ( $n=1$ ) to an excited state ( $n=3$ ) from which it can then transition to $n=2$ , emitting radiation observable as part of the Balmer series.

questions.question_html: Radius of a certain orbit of hydrogen atom is 8.48 $\overset{o}{A}$ . If energy of electron in this orbit is $E/x$ . then $x=$ ________ (Given $a_{0}=0.529$ $\overset{o}{A}$ , $E=$ energy of electron in ground state).
questions.explanation_text: Let's approach this problem by understanding the basics and applying the Bohr model to find the energy levels of a hydrogen atom. The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom for any given orbit can be defined using the formula: $E_{n}=\frac{E}{n^{2}}$ where: $E$ is the energy of the electron in the ground state ( $n=1$ ), and $n$ is the principal quantum number (orbit number). The radius of an orbit in the hydrogen atom, according to the Bohr model, is given by: $r_{n}=n^{2}a_{0}$ where: $r_{n}$ is the radius of the nth orbit, $a_{0}$ is the Bohr radius ( $0.529$ angstroms or $\overset{o}{A}$ ), and $n$ is the principal quantum number (orbit number). Given that: The radius of a certain orbit of the hydrogen atom is $8.48\overset{o}{A}$ , and The energy of an electron in this orbit is $E/x$ , We need to find $x$ . First, let's find $n$ , the principal quantum number for the orbit with radius $8.48$ angstroms: $8.48=n^{2} \times 0.529$ Solving for $n^{2}$ : $n^{2}=\frac{8.48}{0.529}$ $n^{2} \approx 16.03$ For simplicity and practicality in the quantum model, $n^{2}$ approximately equal to 16 would imply $n=4$ , considering $n$ must be a whole number and $16.03$ is close to $16$ , which is a perfect square of $4$ . Now, to find $x$ , we'll use the energy relationship. Since the energy levels of the hydrogen atom are inversely proportional to the square of the principal quantum number $n$ , $E_{orbit}=\frac{E}{n^{2}}=\frac{E}{4^{2}}=\frac{E}{16}$ According to the given information, $E_{orbit}=\frac{E}{x}$ , which means: $\frac{E}{x}=\frac{E}{16}$ Hence, $x=16$

According to the given information, $E_{orbit}=\frac{E}{x}$ , which means:

questions.explanation_text: To determine the energy equivalent of a mass, we use Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle given by the equation: $E=mc^{2}$ where: - $E$ is the energy - $m$ is the mass - $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, which is approximately $3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ Given the mass $m=1g=1 \times 10^{-3}kg$ , we can substitute these values into the equation: $E=(1 \times 10^{-3}kg) \times (3 \times 10^{8}m/s)^{2}$ Calculating this, we get: $E=1 \times 10^{-3} \times 9 \times 10^{16}$ $E=9 \times 10^{13}J$ Next, to convert this energy into electron volts ( $eV$ ), we use the conversion factor: $1J=6.242 \times 10^{12}MeV$ . Therefore: $E=9 \times 10^{13}J \times 6.242 \times 10^{12}MeV/J$ Calculating this, we get: $E=5.6178 \times 10^{26}MeV$ Therefore, the energy equivalent of $1g$ of a substance is: Option A: $5.6 \times 10^{26}MeV$

$E=mc^{2}$

where:

- $E$ is the energy

- $m$ is the mass

- $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, which is approximately $3 \times 10^{8}m/s$

Given the mass $m=1g=1 \times 10^{-3}kg$ , we can substitute these values into the equation:

$E=(1 \times 10^{-3}kg) \times (3 \times 10^{8}m/s)^{2}$

Calculating this, we get:

$E=1 \times 10^{-3} \times 9 \times 10^{16}$

$E=9 \times 10^{13}J$

Next, to convert this energy into electron volts ( $eV$ ), we use the conversion factor: $1J=6.242 \times 10^{12}MeV$ .

Therefore:

$E=9 \times 10^{13}J \times 6.242 \times 10^{12}MeV/J$

Calculating this, we get:

$E=5.6178 \times 10^{26}MeV$

Therefore, the energy equivalent of $1g$ of a substance is:

Option A: $5.6 \times 10^{26}MeV$

questions.question_html: The longest wavelength associated with Paschen series is : (Given $R_{H}=1.097 \times 10^{7}SI$ unit)
questions.explanation_text: To determine the longest wavelength associated with the Paschen series, we need to understand what the Paschen series is and how its wavelength can be calculated. The Paschen series pertains to the spectral line emissions of the hydrogen atom as an electron transitions from higher energy levels (n > 3) down to n = 3. The formula used to calculate the wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the emitted photon during such a transition in the hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R_{H}(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{n^{2}})$ where, $R_{H}$ is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen, $R_{H}=1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{m}^{-1}$ . $n$ is the principal quantum number of the higher energy level (For the longest wavelength, we use the smallest possible value of $n$ that is larger than 3, which is $n=4$ , since for longer wavelength transitions, the difference in energy levels should be the smallest). To find the longest wavelength, we plug in $n=4$ into the Rydberg equation, as this corresponds to the smallest energy transition within the Paschen series ( $n=4$ to $n=3$ ): $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16})$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{16-9}{144})$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}=76403.47\text{m}^{-1}$ Finally, we calculate $\lambda$ by taking the reciprocal of this value: $\lambda=\frac{1}{76403.47} \approx 1.308 \times 10^{-5}\text{m}=1.308 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{2}\text{cm}=1.308 \times 10^{-3}\text{cm}$ It seems there was a mistake in my calculation. Revising the calculation properly: $\lambda=\frac{1}{1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}}$ Correctly evaluating this, we should directly compute: $\lambda \approx \frac{144}{7 \times 1.097 \times 10^{7}}=\frac{144}{7.679 \times 10^{7}} \approx 1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{m}$ Therefore, the correct option that matches our calculation for the longest wavelength in the Paschen series is: Option B: $1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{m}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the longest wavelength associated with the Paschen series, we need to understand what the Paschen series is and how its wavelength can be calculated. The Paschen series pertains to the spectral line emissions of the hydrogen atom as an electron transitions from higher energy levels (n > 3) down to n = 3. The formula used to calculate the wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the emitted photon during such a transition in the hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula:

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R_{H}(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{n^{2}})$

where,

  • $R_{H}$ is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen, $R_{H}=1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{m}^{-1}$ .
  • $n$ is the principal quantum number of the higher energy level (For the longest wavelength, we use the smallest possible value of $n$ that is larger than 3, which is $n=4$ , since for longer wavelength transitions, the difference in energy levels should be the smallest).

To find the longest wavelength, we plug in $n=4$ into the Rydberg equation, as this corresponds to the smallest energy transition within the Paschen series ( $n=4$ to $n=3$ ):

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}})$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16})$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7}(\frac{16-9}{144})$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}$

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}=76403.47\text{m}^{-1}$

Finally, we calculate $\lambda$ by taking the reciprocal of this value:

$\lambda=\frac{1}{76403.47} \approx 1.308 \times 10^{-5}\text{m}=1.308 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{2}\text{cm}=1.308 \times 10^{-3}\text{cm}$

It seems there was a mistake in my calculation. Revising the calculation properly:

$\lambda=\frac{1}{1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \frac{7}{144}}$

Correctly evaluating this, we should directly compute:

$\lambda \approx \frac{144}{7 \times 1.097 \times 10^{7}}=\frac{144}{7.679 \times 10^{7}} \approx 1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{m}$

Therefore, the correct option that matches our calculation for the longest wavelength in the Paschen series is:

Option B: $1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{m}$ .

questions.question_text: According to Bohr's theory, the moment of momentum of an electron revolving in $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit of hydrogen atom is:
questions.question_html: According to Bohr's theory, the moment of momentum of an electron revolving in $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit of hydrogen atom is:
questions.explanation_text: According to Bohr's theory, one of the postulates specifies that the angular momentum of an electron in orbit around a nucleus is quantized. This quantization can be expressed by the formula: $L=n\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$ Where: $L$ is the angular momentum of the electron, $n$ is the principal quantum number (or the orbit number in simpler terms), which can take positive integer values (1, 2, 3, ...), $ℎ$ is Planck's constant ( $6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}m^{2}kg/s$ ), and $\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$ is often denoted as $ℏ$ (h-bar), known as the reduced Planck's constant. For an electron in the 4th orbit ( $n=4$ ) of a hydrogen atom, we substitute $n=4$ into the equation: $L=4\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$ Therefore, the moment of momentum (or angular momentum) of an electron in the $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is: $L=4\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}=2\frac{2ℎ}{2\pi}=2\frac{ℎ}{\pi}$ Hence, the correct option is: Option A: $2\frac{ℎ}{\pi}$
questions.explanation_html:
According to Bohr's theory, one of the postulates specifies that the angular momentum of an electron in orbit around a nucleus is quantized. This quantization can be expressed by the formula:

$L=n\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$

Where:

  • $L$ is the angular momentum of the electron,
  • $n$ is the principal quantum number (or the orbit number in simpler terms), which can take positive integer values (1, 2, 3, ...),
  • $ℎ$ is Planck's constant ( $6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}m^{2}kg/s$ ), and
  • $\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$ is often denoted as $ℏ$ (h-bar), known as the reduced Planck's constant.

For an electron in the 4th orbit ( $n=4$ ) of a hydrogen atom, we substitute $n=4$ into the equation:

$L=4\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}$

Therefore, the moment of momentum (or angular momentum) of an electron in the $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is:

$L=4\frac{ℎ}{2\pi}=2\frac{2ℎ}{2\pi}=2\frac{ℎ}{\pi}$

Hence, the correct option is:

Option A: $2\frac{ℎ}{\pi}$

questions.question_html: The radius of third stationary orbit of electron for Bohr's atom is R. The radius of fourth stationary orbit will be:
questions.explanation_text: The radius of the nth stationary orbit in the Bohr model of an atom is directly proportional to the square of its principal quantum number n and inversely proportional to the atomic number Z. This relationship is represented by the formula $r_{n}=\frac{n^{2}ℎ^{2}}{4\pi^{2}kme^{2}Z},$ where : $n$ is the principal quantum number, $ℎ$ is Planck's constant, $k$ is the Coulomb constant, $m$ is the mass of the electron, $e$ is the charge of the electron, and $Z$ is the atomic number of the nucleus (for hydrogen, Z=1). To find the radius of the fourth orbit ( $r_{4}$ ), in comparison to the third orbit ( $r_{3}$ ), we apply the formula with $n=4$ for the fourth orbit and $n=3$ for the third orbit, and simplify as follows: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{r_{4}}{r_{3}}=\frac{(4^{2})ℎ^{2}}{4\pi^{2}kme^{2}Z} \div \frac{(3^{2})ℎ^{2}}{4\pi^{2}kme^{2}Z}=\frac{(4^{2})}{(3^{2})} \\ \\ & =\frac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$ Thus, the radius of the fourth stationary orbit is $\frac{16}{9}$ times the radius of the third stationary orbit, $R$ . Therefore, $r_{4}=\frac{16}{9}R$ .

The emission frequency of radiation from a hydrogen-like ion during electron transitions can be understood using the formula derived from Rydberg's equation for hydrogen-like atoms, which is given as:

$E= rac{E_{0}}{ℎ}( rac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}- rac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$

where:

  • $E$ is the energy of the emitted photon,
  • $E_{0}$ is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen,
  • $ℎ$ is Planck's constant,
  • $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are the principal quantum numbers for the initial and final energy levels, respectively, with $n_{2}<n_{1}$ .

Given a transition from $n=2$ to $n=1$ emits radiation with a frequency of $3 imes 10^{15}Hz$ , we can write:

$ u_{1}=3 imes 10^{15}Hz$

For the transition from $n=3$ to $n=1$ , we can use the same principle to find the frequency of the emitted radiation, $ u_{2}$ , which will depend on the difference in energy levels involved in the transition. The frequency is directly proportional to this energy difference, so we can compare the two transitions using their respective frequencies:

$ rac{ u_{2}}{ u_{1}}= rac{( rac{1}{n_{1f}^{2}}- rac{1}{n_{1i}^{2}})}{( rac{1}{n_{2f}^{2}}- rac{1}{n_{2i}^{2}})}= rac{( rac{1}{1^{2}}- rac{1}{3^{2}})}{( rac{1}{1^{2}}- rac{1}{2^{2}})}= rac{(1- rac{1}{9})}{(1- rac{1}{4})}$

After simplification:

$ rac{ u_{2}}{3 imes 10^{15}}= rac{( rac{8}{9})}{( rac{3}{4})}= rac{32}{27}$

Thus, to find the frequency $u_{2}$ for the transition from $n=3$ to $n=1$ :

$ u_{2}= rac{32}{9} imes 10^{15}Hz$

Hence, in the given formula $ rac{x}{9} imes 10^{15}Hz$ for the frequency, $x$ is equal to $32$ .

questions.question_text: In a nuclear fission process, a high mass nuclide $(A \approx 236)$ with binding energy $7.6MeV/$ Nucleon dissociated into middle mass nuclides $(A \approx 118)$ , having binding energy of $8.6MeV/Nucleon$ . The energy released in the process would be ______ $MeV$ .
questions.question_html: In a nuclear fission process, a high mass nuclide $(A \approx 236)$ with binding energy $7.6MeV/$ Nucleon dissociated into middle mass nuclides $(A \approx 118)$ , having binding energy of $8.6MeV/Nucleon$ . The energy released in the process would be ______ $MeV$ .
questions.explanation_text: To determine the energy released in a nuclear fission process, we use the difference in binding energy (BE) before and after the fission. The formula for energy released ( $Q$ value) in the process is given by: $Q=(\text{Total BE of products})-(\text{Total BE of reactants})$ In this case, the reactant is a high mass nuclide with atomic mass $A \approx 236$ and a binding energy of $7.6MeV/nucleon$ . Each of the two middle mass nuclides formed as products has atomic mass $A \approx 118$ and a binding energy of $8.6MeV/nucleon$ . Therefore, we calculate the total binding energy of reactant and products as follows: For reactant: $\text{BE}_{\text{reactant}}=236 \times 7.6MeV$ For products (since there are two identical products): $\text{BE}_{\text{products}}=2 \times (118 \times 8.6)MeV$ Thus, the energy released ( $Q$ value) is: $Q=\text{BE}_{\text{products}}-\text{BE}_{\text{reactant}}$ $Q=2(118 \times 8.6)-(236 \times 7.6)$ $Q=236 \times (8.6-7.6)$ $Q=236 \times 1$ $Q=236MeV$ This calculation demonstrates how the difference in binding energy per nucleon before and after fission leads to the release of energy, consistent with the mass-energy equivalence principle.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the energy released in a nuclear fission process, we use the difference in binding energy (BE) before and after the fission. The formula for energy released ( $Q$ value) in the process is given by:

$Q=(\text{Total BE of products})-(\text{Total BE of reactants})$

In this case, the reactant is a high mass nuclide with atomic mass $A \approx 236$ and a binding energy of $7.6MeV/nucleon$ . Each of the two middle mass nuclides formed as products has atomic mass $A \approx 118$ and a binding energy of $8.6MeV/nucleon$ .

Therefore, we calculate the total binding energy of reactant and products as follows:

For reactant:

$\text{BE}_{\text{reactant}}=236 \times 7.6MeV$

For products (since there are two identical products):

$\text{BE}_{\text{products}}=2 \times (118 \times 8.6)MeV$

Thus, the energy released ( $Q$ value) is:

$Q=\text{BE}_{\text{products}}-\text{BE}_{\text{reactant}}$

$Q=2(118 \times 8.6)-(236 \times 7.6)$

$Q=236 \times (8.6-7.6)$

$Q=236 \times 1$

$Q=236MeV$

This calculation demonstrates how the difference in binding energy per nucleon before and after fission leads to the release of energy, consistent with the mass-energy equivalence principle.
